content: The World Health Organization (WHO) Regional Office for Europe has developed a comprehensive plan to accelerate the elimination of measles and rubella in the region by 2015. This plan emphasizes the importance of achieving high vaccination coverage, strengthening surveillance systems, and addressing immunity gaps in susceptible populations. 1. Vaccination Strategies: The elimination of measles and rubella requires the administration of two doses of the combined measles and rubella vaccine as part of routine childhood immunization programs. High vaccination coverage (≥95%) must be achieved and maintained across all subnational administrative levels to interrupt disease transmission. Supplementary immunization activities (SIAs) may be necessary to target populations with inadequate immunity, such as under-vaccinated birth cohorts, school and university students, military personnel, and healthcare workers. 2. Surveillance Systems: Robust surveillance systems are essential to detect and classify every suspected case of measles and rubella. This includes timely laboratory investigations and virus genotyping. Many countries in the region still face challenges in establishing reliable surveillance systems for rubella and congenital rubella syndrome (CRS). 3. Challenges in Rubella Elimination: Rubella has a lower infectivity compared to measles, and a single dose of the rubella vaccine provides long-term protection in over 95% of cases. However, up to 50% of rubella cases may present without typical clinical symptoms, complicating timely diagnosis and laboratory confirmation. 4. Immunization System Strengthening: National immunization systems must be capable of reaching at least 95% of the target population with two doses of measlesand rubella-containing vaccines. Immunization programs should be integrated into broader health systems to ensure sustainability and equitable access. 5. Technical and Financial Support: The WHO Regional Office will assist Member States in addressing programmatic and financial challenges, ensuring sustained investments in immunization even after donor support ends. Support will also be provided to improve vaccine management, cold chain logistics, and data quality for immunization coverage monitoring. 6. National Immunization Technical Advisory Groups (NITAGs): NITAGs play a critical role in providing evidence-based recommendations on immunization policies, vaccine schedules, and strategies to reach susceptible populations. Currently, 35 Member States in the European Region have established NITAGs, but approximately one-third of countries still lack these advisory groups. 7. Outbreak Preparedness and Response: Measles and rubella outbreaks have been reported in several countries, highlighting the need for improved outbreak prevention and response mechanisms. The WHO will work with Member States to identify and target age cohorts or subpopulations requiring SIAs, particularly in response to outbreaks or surveillance findings. 8. Verification of Elimination: A verification process has been initiated to confirm the absence of endemic measles and rubella in the region. This process is modeled after the successful polio verification efforts. If high-quality surveillance systems demonstrate no endemic transmission for three consecutive years (2015–2018), elimination can be officially documented and declared by 2018. 9. Call for Accelerated Action: To meet the 2015 elimination target, greater political commitment and accelerated actions are required from Member States, supported by WHO and international partners. The WHO has identified priority areas for technical support and established indicators and milestones to measure progress. 10. Innovative Approaches: Recognizing that traditional methods may not suffice, the plan incorporates innovative strategies to boost vaccine demand and ensure equitable access. Efforts include training health staff, improving immunization information systems, and introducing electronic immunization registries. 11. Milestones and Training: Key milestones include training national coordinators on immunization strategies, assessing vaccine management systems, and promoting the establishment of effective NITAGs in all Member States. Regional training sessions will facilitate the sharing of experiences and best practices among countries. 12. Sustainability and Ownership: The plan emphasizes the importance of country ownership and stewardship in achieving immunization goals. Member States are encouraged to align their national immunization plans with broader health policies and budgets to ensure long-term sustainability. By addressing these critical areas, the WHO Regional Office for Europe aims to eliminate measles and rubella in the region, ensuring better health outcomes for all populations.
